questions.stem: Match the CONVENTION with its PRIMARY concern. A. Ramsar. B. CITES. C. Basel. D. Stockholm. List-II: 1. Hazardous-waste trans-boundary movement. 2. Persistent Organic Pollutants. 3. Wetlands of international importance. 4. International trade in endangered species.
questions.explanation: Ramsar (1971, Iran) — wetlands. CITES (1973, Washington DC) — trade in endangered species. Basel (1989) — transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. Stockholm (2001) — persistent organic pollutants (POPs like DDT, PCBs, dioxins).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Consider the following about the PARIS AGREEMENT (2015). 1. Each Party submits Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) which are internationally binding emission targets. 2. The long-term goal is to keep the global temperature rise well below 2°C, preferably 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. 3. The agreement entered into force in November 2016. 4. Developed countries are obliged to provide at least USD 100 billion per year in climate finance, a goal extended to 2025 at COP26 Glasgow. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is WRONG — NDCs are self-determined and internationally communicated but NOT legally binding as to achievement (only the reporting/updating is binding). This is the famous 'bottom-up' design of Paris. Statements 2, 3, 4 are correct.

questions.stem: The MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987) is notable for:

options.option_text: First global agreement on greenhouse-gas emissions
Universal ratification and successful phase-out of ozone-depleting substances
Covering only industrialised nations, excluding developing ones

questions.explanation: Montreal Protocol is the ONLY UN treaty with universal (198 party) ratification, and it successfully phased out CFCs and related ODS. The 2016 KIGALI AMENDMENT extended its scope to HFCs (powerful greenhouse gases) — but the core protocol was about ozone, not climate.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: India's COMMITMENT under Paris NDCs (updated 2022) INCLUDES:

options.option_text: Reducing emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030
Achieving 50% cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil fuel resources by 2030

questions.explanation: All three are India's updated NDC commitments. 45 % intensity reduction vs 2005 (earlier 33-35 %). 50 % non-fossil installed capacity by 2030. Net-zero by 2070 (announced at COP26 Glasgow 2021). Also: create additional 2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent carbon sink via additional forest and tree cover by 2030.

questions.stem: ASSERTION (A): Ocean acidification is a direct consequence of rising atmospheric CO₂ levels. REASON (R): A fraction of the CO₂ absorbed by seawater forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺ ions, lowering the ocean's pH.

options.option_text: Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.explanation: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. The H⁺ release drops pH. Ocean pH has fallen from ~8.2 (pre-industrial) to ~8.1 today — a ~30 % increase in acidity (pH is logarithmic). Damages coral reefs and shell-forming plankton (pteropods), with cascading effects on marine food webs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of India's 18 BIOSPHERE RESERVES?
questions.explanation: Gir (Gujarat) is a National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary famous for Asiatic lions — but it is NOT one of India's 18 designated Biosphere Reserves. Nilgiri (first designated, 1986), Sundarbans, and Great Nicobar are all Biosphere Reserves under the Indian government programme (and on the UNESCO MAB network).

questions.stem: Consider the following about the KYOTO PROTOCOL (1997). 1. It introduced legally binding emission reduction targets for developed (Annex I) countries for the first commitment period 2008-2012. 2. It was based on the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR). 3. The United States signed but never ratified it. 4. The Doha Amendment extended the Protocol to a second commitment period 2013-2020. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: All four correct. Kyoto's binding targets (5.2 % below 1990 levels overall) distinguished it from later bottom-up Paris. CBDR is a core principle of climate governance. US (Clinton) signed 1998 but Senate refused to ratify (Byrd-Hagel resolution, S. Res. 98). Doha Amendment (2012) covered 2013-2020; ratified slowly, with patchy participation — Paris Agreement took over from 2020.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Which of the following is the PRIMARY cause of the 'ozone hole' phenomenon over Antarctica?

options.option_text: Direct emission of ground-level ozone from industry
Chlorine atoms released from chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) catalytically destroying stratospheric O₃ in the polar vortex
Lightning that breaks down oxygen molecules

questions.explanation: Polar stratospheric clouds provide a surface for heterogeneous reactions; when the Antarctic spring sun arrives, Cl (and Br) radicals released from CFCs catalytically destroy ozone. The polar vortex keeps these reactions concentrated over the pole. Recovery expected ~2060s thanks to Montreal Protocol. Ground-level ozone (a pollutant) is a different story from stratospheric ozone (a protective shield).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Nagoya Protocol (2010) is a supplementary agreement to which of the following international conventions?

options.option_text: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, 1992)
Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, signed in 1992)
Vienna Convention for Protection of the Ozone Layer (1985)
CITES — Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species

questions.explanation: The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) of genetic resources is a supplementary protocol to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), adopted in Nagoya, Japan in 2010 and in force since 2014. Option A (UNFCCC) governs climate change, not genetic-resource access. Options C and D are independent standalone conventions unrelated to ABS. Students often confuse 'supplementary protocol to CBD' with CITES since both deal with biodiversity, but CITES is not a CBD protocol.

questions.stem: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) primarily regulates the transboundary movement of which of the following?

options.option_text: Persistent Organic Pollutants listed under the Stockholm Convention
Hazardous wastes shipped from OECD countries to developing nations
Living Modified Organisms (LMOs) produced through modern biotechnology
Commercially traded specimens of CITES-listed endangered species

questions.explanation: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, a CBD supplementary agreement, governs safe handling, transport, and use of Living Modified Organisms — organisms altered through modern biotechnology — that may adversely affect biodiversity or human health. Option A describes Stockholm Convention scope. Option B describes the Basel Convention and its Ban Amendment. Option D describes CITES. A common trap is conflating Cartagena (biosafety/LMOs) with the Nagoya Protocol (genetic resource access), since both are CBD protocols.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Minamata Convention (2013):
1. It specifically targets mercury and mercury compounds.
2. The Convention was formally adopted in Kumamoto, Japan.
3. It imposes a complete ban on all uses of mercury in consumer products by 2020.
4. India ratified the Minamata Convention in 2018.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct: the convention targets mercury pollution; it was adopted at a diplomatic conference in Kumamoto (near Minamata city) in October 2013; India ratified it on 13 September 2018. Statement 3 is wrong — the convention does not impose a blanket ban on all mercury uses; it phases out or restricts specific products (certain batteries, lamps, measuring devices) and industrial processes, while permitting essential uses under exemptions. Confusing a targeted phase-out schedule with a complete prohibition is the standard trap examiners set here.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Rotterdam Convention (1998):
1. It operates through the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure for hazardous chemicals and pesticides.
2. It is jointly administered by UNEP and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
3. A chemical qualifies for Annex III listing only after qualifying notifications from two or more different PIC regions.
4. The Rotterdam Convention was adopted in the same year as the Stockholm Convention.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct: Rotterdam's core mechanism is Prior Informed Consent; it is co-managed by UNEP and FAO (FAO's agricultural expertise covers pesticides); and Annex III listing requires qualifying notifications from at least two different PIC regions, ensuring geographic spread. Statement 4 is wrong — Rotterdam was adopted in 1998 in Rotterdam, Netherlands; the Stockholm Convention was adopted separately in 2001 in Stockholm, Sweden. Conflating these two 'sister chemicals conventions' with the same adoption year is a PYQ-level precision trap.

questions.stem: The Adaptation Fund, which finances concrete climate adaptation projects in developing nations, was established under which legal instrument and draws its primary initial funding from which source?

options.option_text: Under the Paris Agreement (2015), funded by voluntary pledges from Annex-I nations
Under the Kyoto Protocol, funded partly by a 2% levy on CDM project proceeds
Under UNFCCC itself (1992), funded by the Global Environment Facility (GEF)
Under the CBD Nagoya Protocol, funded by ABS compliance fees from bioprospectors

questions.explanation: The Adaptation Fund was established under the Kyoto Protocol and its unique revenue feature is a 2% share of proceeds automatically levied on Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) project revenues — an automatic finance mechanism unlike voluntary pledge-based funds. Option A is wrong: the Paris Agreement's primary finance vehicle is the Green Climate Fund (GCF). Option C is wrong: UNFCCC's core financial mechanism is the GEF; the Adaptation Fund is a Kyoto construct, not a 1992 UNFCCC creation. Option D mixes up two unrelated treaty regimes entirely.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about international environmental conventions:
1. The Basel Convention's Ban Amendment (adopted 1995) entered into force in 2019, prohibiting hazardous waste exports from Annex VII (EU/OECD/Liechtenstein) to non-Annex VII countries.
2. Under the Stockholm Convention, Annex A chemicals are targeted for elimination while Annex B chemicals are subject to restriction.
3. The Vienna Convention (1985) itself set legally binding ODS reduction targets, which the Montreal Protocol subsequently revised.
4. The Waigani Convention bans import of hazardous and radioactive wastes into Pacific Island Forum countries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct: the Basel Ban Amendment entered into force on 5 December 2019 after achieving its required ratifications; Stockholm's Annex A (elimination)/Annex B (restriction)/Annex C (minimisation) structure is precisely as described; the Waigani Convention (1995) is a Pacific regional treaty banning such imports into Forum Island Countries. Statement 3 is wrong — the Vienna Convention (1985) is a framework convention with no binding ODS targets; all legally binding phase-out schedules were created solely by the Montreal Protocol (1987). Attributing Montreal's targets to the Vienna Convention is the classic parent-protocol confusion trap in ozone questions.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) adopted at CBD COP15 in December 2022:
1. It superseded the Aichi Biodiversity Targets under the CBD Strategic Plan 2011–2020.
2. It includes the '30×30' target, aiming to protect at least 30% of land and ocean areas by 2030.
3. It established a mandatory biodiversity loss-and-damage fund parallel to the UNFCCC climate mechanism.
4. It committed to mobilising at least USD 20 billion per year in international biodiversity finance to developing countries by 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct: the GBF replaced the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (2010–2020 strategic plan); the '30×30' area-based conservation commitment (Target 3) is the framework's flagship goal; and the GBF financial package commits USD 20 billion/year to developing nations by 2025, rising to USD 30 billion by 2030. Statement 3 is wrong — the GBF does not establish a mandatory loss-and-damage fund for biodiversity; the UNFCCC loss-and-damage fund was a distinct outcome from COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, November 2022). Blending the UNFCCC COP27 loss-and-damage breakthrough with the CBD COP15 GBF — two major December 2022 outcomes — is a precision trap that targets candidates who follow both negotiations casually.
